opus-5.5.text:
I think the future agent ecosystem will probably be more diverse than people imagine. Many people picture one super-agent that does everything for you. That could happen in some form, but I suspect we'll see several layers coexisting.

One layer is general-purpose assistants, close to what ChatGPT or similar products are becoming. You talk to it, it understands your context, and it can call tools and do things for you. Then there are more specialized agents built around particular environments: coding, research, customer service, and finance. Those environments have their own data, their own feedback signals, and their own ways of judging what "good" looks like. In those settings the moat isn't only the model. It's also the environment, the context, and the reward.

The thing I find most interesting is that the bottleneck is shifting. For a long time the question was whether the model was smart enough. Now models are pretty capable at reasoning, and the harder questions are about the environment and the task. What tasks actually matter? How do you evaluate them? How does an agent get the right context about a person or an organization? How does it keep learning over time instead of starting from zero every conversation? Memory, long-term context, and something like continual learning will be very important for the next stage.

There's also the question of how agents interact with each other and with existing infrastructure. Today most of the digital world was built for humans: websites, apps, interfaces. Over time I'd expect more of it to be built for agents too, with better interfaces and protocols, so agents don't have to imitate a human clicking buttons. That changes how products are designed and possibly how value is distributed.

Personally, I care less about the specific shape and more about utility. The real test is whether these agents create value in the real world, not just high benchmark scores. When an agent can reliably do things that matter economically or in people's lives, the ecosystem will form around that, sometimes in ways nobody planned. So I'm pretty optimistic, but I think we're still early, and the most important work now is defining the right problems, not just solving the ones we already have.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't know the exact shape, but I have a fairly strong intuition about the direction, and it comes from thinking about what an "agent" actually is in the first place.

Right now most people think of agents as products. ChatGPT with tools, Claude Code, Cursor, Manus, whatever. Each one is a closed box. The model is inside, the environment is inside, the memory is inside. And the way we compare them is by benchmarks, which basically measure how well a single box solves a single task from a cold start. That's a very 2023 to 2025 way of thinking, and I think it's going to look naive pretty quickly.

The reason is that intelligence isn't going to be the bottleneck for much longer. The models are getting good enough that the question stops being "can it do the task" and becomes "does it have the right context, the right tools, the right memory, and the right incentives." So the ecosystem will be organized around those things, not around the models.

Concretely, I'd break it into a few layers.

The first layer is environments. When I did SWE-bench and WebShop and the earlier work, the thing I kept noticing was that the environment is where most of the leverage is. If you give an agent a good environment, you get good behavior almost for free. If the environment is bad, no amount of prompting fixes it. So I expect a huge amount of value to accrue to whoever builds the environments that agents live in. Code repositories, browsers, operating systems, scientific instruments, financial systems. The companies that make these legible and actionable to agents become infrastructure, the way AWS became infrastructure.

The second layer is memory and continuity. Today's agents forget everything between sessions, or they have some RAG hack bolted on. The ecosystem I imagine has agents that persist. They remember who you are, what they tried last week, why it failed. That changes the economics. An agent that's been working with you for a year is worth far more than a fresh one, which means switching costs go up and the relationship starts to look less like software and more like hiring.

The third layer, and the one I think people underestimate, is agents interacting with other agents. Not in the cute multi-agent sense where you spin up five copies and call it a team. I mean a real economy. My agent negotiates with your company's agent. A research agent commissions an experiment from a lab agent. There need to be protocols, identity, payment, reputation. Something like what HTTP and TCP/IP did for computers, but for agents. Whoever gets that right shapes everything above it.

And then on top of all this, there's a shift in what the human does. I've said before that I think we're moving from a world where humans do the tasks and AI assists, to a world where AI does the tasks and humans set the goals and judge the outcomes. That means the scarce skill becomes taste. Knowing what's worth doing, knowing when a result is good. Most of the training and evaluation work in the field right now is actually about encoding taste into systems, and I don't think that's going to be fully automated for a long time.

If I had to make one bet, it would be this. In five years the word "agent" will mostly disappear, the same way "website" stopped being an interesting word. Everything will be agentic by default. What people will argue about instead is who controls the environments, who owns the memory, and whose values get encoded in the reward. Those are the real questions, and they're less technical than people in my field would like to admit.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is where we draw the boundary between a model and an agent. Will we have one general-purpose agent that does everything, or many specialized agents that work together? My guess is that we’ll have both. You might interact with one assistant that understands your goals, but behind it there could be different systems handling different tasks.

For that ecosystem to work, agents need more than intelligence. They need access to tools, useful context, and ways to check whether they actually accomplished something. If an agent delegates a task to another agent, how does it evaluate the result? How much access should it give? When should it ask you for help? Those become important design questions.

I’m also curious about how much of today’s software will remain organized around human interfaces. An agent doesn’t necessarily need to click through the same screens we do. Some services could become easier to use through tools directly, while interfaces become more focused on helping people express intent and review outcomes.

So I imagine a gradual transition. Agents will first become useful in tasks where success is relatively easy to verify. As they become more reliable, we’ll give them longer tasks and more autonomy. The interesting part is not just having many agents—it’s making their work dependable enough that people actually want to delegate to them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is where we’ll want general-purpose agents and where we’ll want specialized ones. You could imagine a personal agent that understands your goals and preferences, but it doesn’t necessarily do everything itself. It might work with a coding agent, a research agent, or services that expose particular capabilities.

What’s less clear is how much of that coordination needs to happen between autonomous agents. Sometimes a tool call or a simple workflow is enough. Having more agents doesn’t automatically make a system more useful; it can also make errors harder to diagnose.

So I imagine the ecosystem developing around reliability and delegation. Can an agent describe what it can do, recognize when it needs help, and verify the result it receives? Can users control what information and permissions it shares? If we solve those problems, we could have a fairly diverse ecosystem underneath a very simple user experience: you express what you want, and the system figures out how to get it done, involving you when your judgment is needed.
